task_row_model.query: Given the power series sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n (x-2)^n with limsup_{n\to\infty} |a_n|^{1/n} = 4 and a_0 = 0, what is the radius of convergence and what can be said about convergence at the two endpoints? Explain and give examples of endpoint behavior.

documents.content: A standard way to compute the radius of convergence R of a power series sum a_n (x-c)^n is via the root test: R = 1 / L where L = limsup_{n->infty} |a_n|^{1/n}. This formula follows from applying the root test to the terms |a_n (x-c)^n|^{1/n} = |a_n|^{1/n} |x-c|. If L is finite and positive, the series converges absolutely for |x-c| < 1/L and diverges for |x-c| > 1/L. If L = 0 or infinity, the radius is infinite or zero respectively.

Analytic continuation and Taylor expansions relate to radii of convergence: the radius about a center c equals the distance from c to the nearest singularity of the analytic function represented by the series. This geometric perspective explains why different centers yield different radii. For entire functions there are no finite singularities so the radius is infinite. While this viewpoint is useful for understanding why limsup of coefficients reflects singularities, it does not by itself compute R from a numeric limsup of coefficients.

Endpoint behavior of a power series must be tested separately after computing the radius. When |x-c| equals the radius, terms need not tend to zero, so convergence can fail. Typical tests at endpoints include the alternating series test (Leibniz), comparison with p-series, and Dirichlet/Abel tests when signs or monotonicity appear. For coefficients with polynomial decay multiplied by the critical exponential growth, one can get conditional convergence at one endpoint and divergence at the other. No universal criterion covers all cases; examination of a_n and substitution x = c +/- R is necessary.

Compute R from L = limsup |a_n|^{1/n} = 4 using R = 1/L, so the radius of convergence is R = 1/4. Since the center is 2, the interval of possible real convergence is |x-2| < 1/4, i.e. (1.75, 2.25). The two endpoints are x = 2 +/- 1/4 = 1.75 and 2.25 and must be tested separately. For example, if a_n = 4^n / n then at x = 2.25 the terms are (4^n/n)*(1/4)^n = 1/n so the series diverges; at x = 1.75 the terms are (4^n/n)*(-1/4)^n = (-1)^n / n which converges by the alternating series test. If instead a_n = 4^n / n^2 both endpoints give sum 1/n^2 and converge absolutely. Thus R = 1/4, endpoints depend on the finer behavior of a_n.

Inside the disc of convergence a power series converges uniformly on any closed subinterval strictly inside the radius. Termwise differentiation and integration are valid within that open interval and produce new power series with the same radius. These operations change coefficients by polynomial factors (n or 1/(n+1)) but do not affect the limsup root determining R. While important for analytic manipulation, these facts do not determine endpoint convergence and therefore do not replace direct tests at |x-c| = R.
